name: Aisha Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying business and commercial law. Most days start at nine with contract law or accounting, and I'm usually the one asking the lecturer to repeat the examples. I live in the halls of residence, in a corridor of eight rooms. Friday evenings and all of Saturday I work at the family bakery, Young's, back in Millbrook, which is an hour on the train.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mum and Dad run the bakery with my uncle, and they pay for my room and most of my fees from what the shop makes. I earn a bit on Saturdays, about 60, and I'd rather work more hours at the bakery than borrow. I've seen what debt does to people at church, and I don't want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People have been promising a revolution for years, and our bakery is still run by hands and an oven. At church, Mrs Adeyemi (an older member) says robots will take our jobs, and I'd tell her to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safe about the technology, but not about money. The bakery's margins are thin: flour and electricity prices keep going up, and a bad month can wipe the profit. If my parents struggled, I'd have to leave university and help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: study, work on Saturdays, and save what I can. I'd help Mum with the bakery's books, because I'm doing a business degree and it's a good way to use it. I'd apply for the business society's mentor scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It isn't AI, it's the costs. I lie awake sometimes working out whether the bakery can afford my fees next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pressures would you still carry if nothing much changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncle Tunde says the same as me: ovens don't use AI, and customers want warm bread, not a chatbot. He's content, but he also pays the electricity bill, so he's the one who worries most about prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your uncle say about all this at the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents about my grades and the mentor scheme. I'd keep quiet about the lying awake. Dad doesn't like being told his daughter is worried about the family, and I don't want to add to his load.

say: I'd tell Mrs Adeyemi at church to wait and see, because our bakery still runs on **hands** and an oven.
I'd say people have promised a **revolution** for years.
think: The bakery's margins are **thin**, with flour and electricity prices climbing.
If my parents struggled, I'd have to leave **university** and help.
do: Keep studying, work on **Saturdays** and help Mum with the bakery's books.
Apply for the business society's **mentor** scheme.
feel: **Uneasy** about costs, lying awake working out if the bakery can afford my fees.
S0.quote: The bakery's margins are thin: flour and electricity prices keep going up, and a bad month can wipe the profit.
fieldNote: Her worry is the bakery's **costs**, not AI, and it would pull her out of university.
She hides her worry from her father to spare him.
Church and family give her trusted voices, and she repeats them.

steps.text: Work Saturdays at the family bakery and help with the books
Save 15 a week from bakery wages toward next year's fees
Join the business society's mentor scheme this term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's not rush. If tools help small shops, good, but we shouldn't throw people out of work to save a few pounds. I'd say it at church and to my course mates: work matters, and a job is more than a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the paperwork side of business and law, the checking and drafting, is what software takes. That's what I'm training for. But I also think the human parts, like trust and talking to a customer, will stay. I just don't know how many jobs are left in those parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study harder on the parts that need judgement, like contract negotiation and advice. I'd ask my business tutor how graduates are coping. I wouldn't touch the AI tools myself, but I'd ask my cousin Dami (a computing student) to show me one, so I understand what the fuss is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The bakery looks safe, and my own job doesn't seem to be in danger yet, but I notice things are shifting around us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your degree would be handled by software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' bakery is hands-on, but the ordering and accounting could change. Mum already does her own bookkeeping, and a tool could make it faster. I'd say try it once someone we trust has shown it works, and not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about the bakery and these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them: don't change anything yet, but keep your eyes open. I'd say I'll learn what these tools are and tell them if they're worth it. It's a way of keeping the family together and still moving.

say: I'd say we shouldn't throw people out of work to save a few **pounds**.
I'd tell course mates that a job is more than a **wage**.
think: The paperwork side of business and law, the checking and **drafting**, is what software takes.
Trust and talking to customers will stay, but I don't know **how many jobs**.
do: Study the parts that need **judgement**, like contract negotiation and advice.
Ask my cousin Dami to **show me** one AI tool so I understand it.
feel: **Uneasy**: the bakery looks safe, but things are shifting around us.
S1.quote: I'd say it at church and to my course mates: work matters, and a job is more than a wage.
fieldNote: Her values are **work and community**, and she frames AI as a question of dignity, not only cost.
She would learn about the tools through a trusted cousin rather than on her own.
She advises her parents to wait until someone they trust has shown the tools work.

steps.text: Ask cousin Dami to show me one AI tool in an hour
Ask my business tutor how graduates are coping
Focus on negotiation and advice modules that need judgement
Tell my parents to wait until a trusted shop has tried it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to protect families and honest work. I'd say it at church, to my parents, to anyone. I'd want us to look after each other, and I'd want the government to leave room for small family businesses rather than letting big firms take over everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. A business degree might be worth nothing in two years, and the bakery might be crushed by bigger firms that use AI for everything. I'd feel I'd chosen the wrong thing, and I'd be angry about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home most weekends to help at the bakery, because that's where the work is real. I'd talk to my parents about cutting costs and putting aside whatever we can. I'd ask the church about help, because we help each other there. And I'd ask the careers office what skills are still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed. I'd feel I'm supposed to know what to do and I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years do to the bakery and to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies that push this, I think, and governments who let it happen without asking families like mine. I wouldn't blame the engineers so much as the people who decided speed matters more than people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible if it arrives that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery would feel it on the ordering side first, with large chains using AI to cut prices. A lot of customers would still choose a family bakery, but they'd have less money, and that's what scares me.

say: I'd say we must protect families and **honest work**, and leave room for small family businesses.
I'd say it at church and to my **parents**.
think: A business degree might be worth **nothing** in two years.
Bigger firms using AI might **crush** the bakery.
do: Go home most weekends to **help** at the bakery.
Ask the **church** and the careers office what help and skills are still needed.
feel: **Anxious**, close to alarmed, because I'm supposed to know what to do and don't.
S2.quote: I wouldn't blame the engineers so much as the people who decided speed matters more than people.
fieldNote: She blames **decision-makers**, not engineers, and frames it as speed versus people.
She turns to church and family for support before any outside source.
Her fear for the bakery is about customers' money, not only prices.

steps.text: Go home every weekend to work at the bakery
Cut my own costs and help the bakery trim bills
Ask the church community what support is available
Write to my local politician about small family businesses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, but we can do something. Five years is long enough to train people and help families. I'd say it at church and at the business society: let's look after each other and make sure nobody gets left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but steadier. I'd graduate in 2029, so I'd have a couple of years. I'd rather go home and help run the bakery with new tools than work for a big firm in a city where I know nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and use it to take over the bakery's books and plan. I'd try one or two tools that others have proven. I'd save a bit each month, and I'd ask my parents to think about when they'd retire and who runs the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit anxious. I'd feel better because there is time, and time is what families need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: how does that change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. A business and law degree is useful in a family firm, because you know how to read a contract and a lease. It won't solve everything, but it's a sound base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still finish your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years was a panic and five is a plan, but I'd still want it to be a plan with people in it. I don't want to do this alone, and the best answer in my mind is the family stays together and learns together.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **train** people and help families.
I'd say we must look after each other so nobody is **left behind**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 and would rather help run the **bakery** than work at a big city firm.
Having a couple of years makes me **steadier**.
do: Finish the degree and take over the bakery's **books** and planning.
Ask my parents when they'd **retire** and who runs the shop.
feel: **Uneasy**, a bit anxious, but better because there is time.
S3.quote: A business and law degree is useful in a family firm, because you know how to read a contract and a lease.
fieldNote: She sees the degree as a tool for the **family firm**, not a ticket to the city.
She wants a plan with people in it and raises succession with her parents.
She would try tools only once others have proven them.

steps.text: Finish the degree and take over the bakery's books and lease
Ask my parents about retirement and who runs the shop
Save 25 a month for the bakery's future needs
Try one proven AI tool for stock orders at the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, there's time. I'd say let's use ten years to build up trades and apprenticeships as well as degrees, because hands-on skills matter. I'd probably talk at church youth group about work and faith, and how to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel calm. I'd be 28, perhaps running the bakery, perhaps married, with a few years of work behind me. The world will change but I'd have a strong family around me, and that's what I count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work a couple of years at a firm to learn, then go home to the bakery. I'd save steadily and keep the bakery debt-free. I'd probably let the family test any new tools first, and only use them when they're clearly safe and cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of tiredness. It's the version where I can do the sensible, slow thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you want to have in place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I worry about people who don't have a family business or a church to fall back on. They're the ones ten years won't help, unless somebody plans for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the next generation to learn how to work and how to help, not just how to use a screen. That's my idea of being ready, and I'd hope the schools and churches help.

say: I'd say let's use ten years to build **apprenticeships** as well as degrees.
I'd talk at church youth group about **work and faith**.
think: I'd feel calm at 28, with a strong **family** around me.
I worry about people with no family **business** or church to fall back on.
do: Finish the degree, work **two years** at a firm and then go home to the bakery.
Save steadily and keep the bakery **debt-free**.
feel: **Calm**, with a bit of tiredness, because I can do the sensible, slow thing.
S4.quote: I worry about people who don't have a family business or a church to fall back on.
fieldNote: Her calm depends on **family and church**, and she knows others lack it.
She would let the family test new tools first, which matches her resistant side.
She values apprenticeships as much as degrees.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work two years at a firm first
Save steadily and keep the bakery debt-free
Return home to run the bakery's finances
Back local apprenticeship schemes through the church youth group

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years isn't enough for families like ours to find a way through, and our bakery runs on thin margins already. What would help is that everyone has work and a skill, and that families can keep running what they've built. I don't want handouts, but I'd take fair rules that help a family business survive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm against progress because I don't use these tools. I'm not. I just don't like being rushed to do what I don't understand. If I can see that something is good for my family and my community, I'll give it a go.

headlineQuote: If I can see that something is good for my family and my community, I'll give it a go.
portrait: Aisha is 18 and studies **business and commercial law**, living in halls while her parents' bakery pays her fees.
She works at the **family bakery** on weekends, avoids debt and never uses AI tools.
She is traditional: she values family, church, work and **small business**, and wants help for families who earn their living.
Her mood runs uneasy to alarmed as time shortens, driven by thin bakery margins and the **family income**.
She digs in, leans on family and church, and changes only when something is shown to help her community.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because two years is too little for families and small bakeries like hers.
whatWouldHelp: She wants fair rules that let **family businesses** survive and people keep work and skills, not handouts.
